candidates.name: Benjamin Moses
facts: Currently involved in: Tampa Muay Thai

notes.brother: From their application: Why this major / passion for healthcare
notes.text: When I think of what it means to be healthy, standard textbook definitions fall flat. To me, true health is a visual, moving with freedom, maintaining a connected body with efficient biomechanics, living in sync with one's natural circadian rhythm, and fueling the body with foods that genuinely nourish it. I initially started out as a finance student, but I soon realized that health and longevity are at the core of my personal values. I needed a career path that aligned with what actually mattered to me, I began exploring human movement and healthcare. That search led me to Osteopathic Medicine. Osteopathy immediately resonated with me because it puts these core values directly into practice. Beyond personal alignment, becoming an osteopath fits the life I want to build. It isn't about the money, though it offers a stable career. It's about being part of a community centered on helping others. Connecting with local practitioners here in Tampa showed me how meaningful this work is. They aren't just doing a job; they've built a community through a shared dedication of helping others holistically. I want to become a Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine with a focus on sports medicine and biomechanics. By taking a whole-body approach to movement, recovery, and performance, I want to become a pillar in my community not just helping people stay healthy, but making people human again.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED
notes.text: Joining Mu Epsilon Delta is about finding my people and building a base for my future in healthcare. I’ve noticed that students drawn to MED usually share similar values around health, movement, and longevity. Surrounding myself with peers who view the world through a similar lens matters to me,it makes the pre-med journey feel less like a choir and builds genuine friendships with people I actually like being around.I fully intend to take advantage of the professional development, networking, and mentorship MED offers as I prepare for a career as an osteopath. Other than the career benefits, being an active member is an essential stepping stone for me. Before I can become a reliable pillar for my future patients and community, I need to practice showing up, getting involved, and being a solid, dependable member of a group right now. Honestly, I want to gain strong support, guidance, and a people who I can love to be around.

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring
notes.text: What I bring to Mu Epsilon Delta comes down to a willingness to learn, an open mind, and solid follow through. My biggest driver is just staying open to new ideas and different perspectives. Being willing to step out of my comfort zone and listen to others is what pushed me to pivot from finance and discover my interest in osteopathic medicine. I come in with the mentality of a sponge, soak in everything I can.  After I knew finance wasn't the path for me I considered being a chiropractic, but I sticked to an open mind set and discovered osteopathy which fit my interests more. Even when I knew my career I knew there for more for me to discover, currently I want to have my niche in NKT and moo functional therapy. Yet I still think there's more for me to look at and get interested in.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text: The experience that shaped me most was straining my ACL during my senior year of high school. Balancing a job and living on my own, I relied on running and boxing to stay sane. After the injury, I tried to push through without doing PT, which led to bad compensatory mechanics, a weird limp, and forced me to drop the activities I loved. Being on my feet for work all day made it worse, and the physical limitations took a huge hit on my mental health. Once I moved to Tampa, I started working with a local physical therapist who honestly therapized me just as much as he helped my knee. He listened to what I was going through mentally while getting me back on track physically. Becoming a patient showed me firsthand how much an injury affects every single corner of a person’s life. It gave me real empathy for people struggling with their health and taught me that treating someone means looking at the whole person, not just fixing a joint. That whole experience made me realize the kind of provider I want to be, someone who genuinely understands both the physical and mental side of recovery and helps patients get their lives back.

candidates.name: Blythe Ellsworth

notes.brother: From their application: Why this major / passion for healthcare
notes.text: I love youtube videos, but there came a time where my feed stopped being sims videos and instead crash course and amoeba sisters videos. I realized I had a LOT of questions about the world and was just absolutely fascinated by the human body and all the mysteries inside. I ended up taking AP Bio my senior year and found such a love for the subject. That class was my absolute favorite and I was always excited to learn more and ask more questions. I've never felt that way about a class before. Even if I wasn't planning on pursuing medicine I would still have biology as a major.  I also love helping people---which might sound cliche. Truly nothing is more rewarding to me though than making someone's day better. Medicine is such a broad spectrum with SO many opportunities. I love school and I love learning about the things I'm passionate about. A lot of people will say to me "you're in for a long ride" and things of that nature.. but I truly could not be more excited to learn more, even though it definitely at times will be hard. I struggled a lot with my ADHD throughout school until my senior year when I got diagnosed and started medication. Before this medicine was not even on my mind of ideas for my future. Getting the help I needed opened up my world and made me realize that I was just as a capable as my peers and that I could become a doctor if I really wanted to.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED
notes.text: To me, community is one of the most powerful and important things a person can have. Having a community full of like-minded driven people is something I very much want. I want  people to struggle with , nerd out with, laugh with, learn with, and just be with. Being on a pre-health track can be very isolating and scary. I constantly feel like I'm not doing enough or I'm doing too much. Although we have to do the work ourselves, I think having community throughout the journey is necessary to becoming the best student and hopefully doctor I can be. Besides the community aspect of MED, I hope to gain experience and opportunities in the healthcare field. I wasn't involved in the medical clubs/programs at my school because I didn't realize I was interested in them until my senior year. I always felt behind because of this but I think that MED is an opportunity for me to have that exposure and even more.

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring

I am not afraid to speak up, but I also know when to step back and let someone else’s idea take the lead. I think some of my best ideas come from conversations with other people, and I would bring that same openness and energy to MED. I am someone who will ask questions, get involved, and follow through on an idea rather than just talk about it.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text:
As a lifeguard for three summers and a nanny for four children, I learned how important it is to stay calm and responsible when other people are depending on you. I used first aid in both roles and, as a lifeguard, helped train newer lifeguards. These experiences taught me to pay attention to the people around me and respond when someone needs help. 
As a Hawk PRIDE Commissioner, I helped lead orientation for about 650 freshmen and mentored students. I learned how to make people feel welcome, listen to them, and adjust to different personalities. As a youth group leader, I mentored girls ages 11–18 and made sure everyone felt comfortable speaking up. I also learned how to adjust my approach based on what each person needed. Being a yearbook editor taught me how to manage a team, meet deadlines, and bring different ideas together.

notes.brother: From their application: Why this major / passion for healthcare
notes.text: I chose my major because when I was in high school, I was a member of sports medicine club. I was always told to choose a career path that makes it seem like your job is not a job, yet a hobby. That is what athletic training is to me. I loved the rush of being able to run on the field when someone is down. In a time of panic, I felt comfort. I loved being in that position and feeling the adrenaline run through me. I knew it was what I wanted to do in life, which is why I am an athletic training major. I also am very hard-working. I know that choosing a career in healthcare takes a lot of effort and can be challenging, but I’m willing to work hard to be able to reach my career goals. I think that being a part of this fraternity would also help me learn from the people around me and be able to become a better student and future healthcare professional.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text: In high school I was a part of sports medicine club which really introduced me to the specific field of medicine I want to be in. It taught me how important it is to listen and be there for people. I was able to see how athletic trainer works at a high school level and that helped me get a perspective of what my day to day would look like as an AT. It also helped me get to see injuries at firsthand. At many hospitals, you get to see an injury after it happened however, as an AT you get to see the injury happen and witness how it happened in person which is something many people don’t get to experience. I also was in a pre-health professional club, which helped expose me to various realms of medicine. It also helped give me experience with teamwork and leadership. Throughout competitions, it helped me become more confident and prepared for the challenges of working in healthcare, as well as fully understand that healthcare is about helping and caring for others not just the science behind it.

candidates.name: Brianna Mercado
facts: Familiar with a current brother: No, I do not know any current members.

Currently involved in: On campus, I am involved in: Circle K (Treasure and Student Government Representative, Rock Music Club, Pottery Club, and Roots of Wisdom. Off campus I am an active member of Odyssey of the Mind, as a judge, coach, and...

notes.brother: From their application: Why this major / passion for healthcare
notes.text:
I had no clue what I wanted to do when I applied to college. Like zero clue. But randomly during my senior year, about a month before graduation, after I had already picked my college and everything, I was sitting in my economics class and we got randomly assigned a career to research. I went to the dentist. And I was like, what the heck. But as I started looking into it and looking at the work they do, something just sparked in me.
Because I was already set to be a non-science major, I kind of forgot about it for a bit. But my first semester here at UTampa, I just kept thinking about dentistry, and about becoming a bio major. And I remember sitting at my desk in my dorm and just being like, you know what, I'm gonna do it. I enjoy being able to talk to different people and connect with them, and dentistry lets me do that while also helping people feel good about themselves. And being an artist is a huge part of my life, so I think that's part of it too. Dentistry lets me stay connected to that side of me without actually being an artist. It's kind of like the art field of the med world, there's real creativity and precision in it, and that lines up with who I am. And I really just want to be able to make people smile. Like literally. With dentistry, people kind of hate the process, nobody loves getting braces or sitting through appointments. But once you're finished, people get so happy. And that happiness is what I want to bring to people and be a part of.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED
notes.text: What I'm hoping to gain most from MED is friendship with people who have the same drive to go into the dental field that I do. This process can feel overwhelming, especially without anyone around you going through the same thing. I haven't taken many STEM courses yet, but even in the classes I have taken, I noticed a huge difference between the times I didn't know anyone and the times I had even one or two friends in the room. Having someone else there made a hard class feel approachable instead of miserable, and I think that applies on a much bigger scale relating to the pre-health journey. I'm also hoping to gain connections and shadowing opportunities, since I know I still need more exposure to the dental field. But what draws me to MED the most is being around people who actually understand how stressful this can be, because they're living it too. It's one thing to have friends who are supportive in general, but it's different to have friends who understand exactly why you're stressed about a DAT timeline or a research application, because it's something they're going through as well. Being around people with that same drive would push me to work harder and it would make the process less lonely. Having people I can lean on, vent to, and grow alongside would make the next three years feel less like just trying to pass my classes and more like building my future.

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring
notes.text: One of the biggest things I would bring to MED is just being approachable. I tend to be someone people feel comfortable coming up to, whether it's to ask a question, vent about something stressful, or just talk. Even in classes, I've noticed people I don't know very well will come sit next to me or start a conversation, which tells me people generally feel safe approaching me pretty quickly. In an organization like MED, where everyone is taking difficult STEM courses and applying to research opportunities, I think having people around who feel easy to talk to actually matters a lot. Not everything needs to be serious or high-stakes all the time just because we are pre-medical, and I think my personality helps balance that out. Along with that, I'd say compassion is probably my strongest trait. If someone wants to talk, whether it's about something going on in their life or just needing to vent about a bad exam, I'm someone who will actually sit and listen instead of brushing it off.This comes through most in my experience coaching and mentoring younger kids, where I've had to learn to actually pay attention to what someone needs instead of just hearing what they're saying. Whether it's a kid who's frustrated because something isn't working, or one who's just having an off day, I've learned that most of the time people just want to feel heard before anything else. Overall, I think what I'd bring to MED is a friendly face, someone who knows how to be professional and get things done, but who's also approachable and easy to talk to.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text:
Odyssey of the Mind, a creative problem-solving organization, has shaped how I approach problems for the past three years. Competing taught me how to break down overwhelming challenges into small, manageable pieces, and how to be resourceful when resources were limited, skills that helped my team reach multiple state finals and in 2025, 5th place in World Finals. Since then, I've moved into coaching and judging. Coaching a team of first graders has tested my patience in a way competing never did, and having to explain the same idea five different ways until it finally clicks has taught me a lot about how differently people learn, something I think will matter a lot when it comes to explaining treatment plans to patients someday. Judging at regional competitions has also pushed me to evaluate people's work fairly and give feedback that's actually constructive. And because I was once a nervous, overwhelmed competitor myself, I genuinely understand what participants are going through, which has made me a more patient and compassionate person.
My involvement in Circle K, a volunteer club at UTampa, has taught me something different. I became one of the club's first members after Dr. Dobrinski, a biology professor I'm close with, encouraged her students to start it. Since then, I've gotten to watch it grow from the ground up. This semester, as both Treasurer and Student Government Representative, I'm in charge of allocating funds for events like awareness walks and donation drives, and keeping our club updated on funding and policy changes across campus. It's pushed me to be more organized and dependable, and I'm especially excited to help lead an initiative working with foster care children this semester. All of these experiences have prepared me for dentistry in many ways. Dentistry isn't just about clinical skill, it's also a lot of talking; like having to explain a procedure to a nervous patient, walking a parent through their kid's treatment plan, or just making someone feel comfortable in a place they don't want to be. Coaching and judging have made me comfortable talking to people of all ages, and Circle K has helped me get better at leading a room and explaining things clearly. I think leadership and compassion really go hand in hand. Being a good dentist means having patients actually trust you, and that trust comes from being approachable and caring, not just being technically skilled.

candidates.name: Cate Wells
facts: Familiar with a current brother: Ariana Kumar - President's Leadership Fellows

notes.brother: From their application: Why this major / passion for healthcare
notes.text: My love for biology began in my 8th grade science class. Mr. Czajkowski had us dissecting frogs, diagnosing mystery illnesses in "patients" played by fellow classmates, and unraveling the Krebs cycle. My curiosity grew through the AP Biology and Anatomy and Physiology classes I took in high school, and I'm ready to dive deeper at the collegiate level. How the body works and adapts to survive, paired with how we treat our bodies, fascinates me. My drive toward healthcare comes from my personal experience. When my grandmother was diagnosed with cancer, I helped care for her in small ways, bringing her water, reading to her, just being present. Although she was in pain, her smile from my tiny gestures was the "medicine" she needed. Losing Gram was heartbreaking, but it showed me who I wanted to become. The pain I felt lit a fire and turned that sadness into purpose. Combining my curiosity for the human body with my passion for helping others points to a future in healthcare and dentistry. You may be wondering, why dentistry? I'm not entirely sure, but I've always felt driven toward this field. Shadowing over the summer, I got to see how biology and hands-on skill came together in real time, and I saw the lasting, strong relationships between patients and their dentist, which I found rewarding. Dentistry will let me specialize in one focused area rather than juggling every part of the body. Dentistry offers the opportunity to explore the business side of medicine and one day open my own practice. I loved watching crowns being made and seeing how small details in someone's mouth can make such a huge impact on their confidence and health.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED
notes.text: I hope to gain early exposure to professional development and mentorship. Working alongside like-minded peers who share my academic drive and love for community service would help me grow both as a leader and as a person. I hope to build lifelong friendships through MED, a place where I don't feel alone if I'm facing personal or academic challenges. I want to strengthen my resume, get an early start preparing for the DAT by gaining access to study materials sooner, and refine and sharpen my personal statement. Additionally, I'm looking to build my public speaking skills and take on a mock interview to prepare for future opportunities. Through MED, I hope to continue building my time management skills and developing more efficient study habits, while setting goals I can work toward and see accomplished during my time in Tampa, such as shadowing at a local dental practice and becoming more involved in the community here. Further down the road, I hope to take the knowledge and experience I gain through MED and use it to mentor younger classmen.

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring
notes.text: Throughout high school, I was part of numerous organizations, no matter how big or small the event was, I gave 100 percent of my time and effort. Whether that meant helping direct drills for teammates during basketball practices or tutoring every Saturday at SEAL Literacy Club, showing up in small ways matters and makes an impact. I bring communication and organization skills to the table as well. Through the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society (LLS) Campaign, I worked with local business owners, planned fundraising events, and texted countless family and friends to raise money for research and support for families fighting cancer. I set up a raffle campaign at a local restaurant, promoted it through social media and flyers with QR codes, and personally sold raffle tickets during March Madness games. We raised $4,000 for LLS, which taught me how to set goals, assign tasks, and follow through as a team. Additionally, I built communication skills through the Spartan Stars Board, working alongside the vice principal to create presentations for the club. These were later turned into weekly lessons for freshmen, covering topics such as involvement, respect, and academic success. This process pushed me to communicate more effectively and adapt to who I was talking with, whether it be an underclassman or the principal. Lastly, I would bring compassion into MED. Through the National Honor Society, I supported students with disabilities and helped lead freshman orientation, making people feel welcomed. I came from a private grade school knowing very few people when I entered high school, so I had to put myself out there in a new environment. I know what it feels like to be lonely or shy, but I've always been kind and welcoming. Through MED, I'd be that familiar face for someone who is looking to make friends, helping them feel at home.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text: Working as a food runner in a high-demand, fast-paced environment taught me to multitask in a quick and efficient way. Whether it was serving customers their orders, refilling drinks, grabbing utensils, filling the ice buckets throughout the restaurant or restocking items, I had to do it all in addition to dealing with friendly and not so happy people. This kept me sharp and engaged which will help better equip me for a future in healthcare. notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text:
I haven't worked a large variety of jobs throughout my lifetime, but the ones I have worked have certainly prepared me for a career in healthcare. I was a shift lead at my local juice shop for several years, and I learned how to communicate and lead effectively. These skills are vital in healthcare, especially as an aspiring vet. Through my shadowing opportunities, I've seen how the veterinarian has to communicate with the vet techs and assistants to ensure a surgery goes smoothly. Additionally, the customer service I learned is important for relating to clients. Explaining details such as prices and health benefits parallels vet med because I can better explain how much a medicine or procedure will cost and how it will help their animal. Additionally, lifeguarding has taught me the importance of teamwork and quick response. In training, we practice saves where all of us lifeguards have to work together to save a victim. For example, someone is responsible for the AED, someone is responsible for compressions, someone is responsible for oxygen, and someone is responsible for the crowd. This life-saving teamwork is very similar to the setup I have seen at veterinary practices. Each person has a job and communicates with each other under high-stakes circumstances. These skills are necessary for a career in healthcare. Also, running cross country and track competitively in high school taught me how to excel under pressure. My team won multiple state championships, and being a top runner on a state-contending team taught me how to control adrenaline and stay focused. Harnessing adrenaline is an essential skill for the life-saving responsibilities associated with healthcare.
All of these skills, in addition to my shelter volunteering and shadowing experience, have made me significantly more prepared for a healthcare career than I ever thought I would be.

notes.brother: From their application: Why this major / passion for healthcare
notes.text:
Why I chose biology stems from an appreciation for the sheer elegance of human physiology. Studying life at both the cellular and systemic levels reveals how carefully balanced our bodies are—and how profound it is when that balance must be restored. Medicine bridges that scientific curiosity with direct human impact. Whether managing everyday preventative care or facing the high-stakes precision of neurosurgery, the chance to understand the human body and use that knowledge to alter the course of a patient’s life is what anchors my commitment to the pre-med track.
What fuels my passion for healthcare, however, extends beyond the science to a dire need for systemic advocacy. Today’s healthcare landscape has patients being left vulnerable, severe staffing shortages, administrative barriers, and insurance denials that jeopardize critical care way too often. Watching patients suffer from systemic failures rather than clinical limitations creates an evident call to action.
To me, being a physician means refusing to accept these breakdowns as unavoidable. It means dedicating 100% effort to help even a single person reclaim their quality of life, while actively advocating for equitable access and patient-first care. I want to become a physician who combines clinical excellence with steadfast patient advocacy—one who not only delivers top-tier treatment in the OR or clinic, but also fights within the system to ensure patients actually receive the care they deserve.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED
notes.text:
The pre-med path is something you really have to grind for. Whether it’s endless hours in the library, stressing over lab reports, and checking off boxes for medical school applications, if you don’t grind, you don’t shine. What I’m hoping to gain from MED isn’t just adding it to my resume, but finding a real community that keeps that journey centered.
I hope to gain the camaraderie of peers who genuinely understand the pressure and share the same drive. It’s one thing to study organic chemistry or prep for the MCAT alone; it’s entirely different to do it with people who hold you accountable, celebrate your wins, and help you shake off your setbacks. I’m looking for honest guidance from upperclassmen who walked this road before, and I want to be that person for others coming up behind me.
Just as importantly, I want to get out of the classroom and actually do the work. Medicine isn’t theoretical—it’s about people. Getting involved in community service alongside brothers who care as much about patient impact as academic performance will keep my focus where it needs to be: on serving others with empathy, humility, and purpose.
Ultimately, I want to join MED to grow into a well-rounded clinician. I want the late-night study sessions, the difficult conversations, the mentorship, and the shared purpose. I’m hoping to gain brothers who challenge my perspective, push me to be a better leader, and remind me why I chose this path in the first place.

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring
notes.text:
What I bring to MED is technical focus, logistical competence, and clear communication.
 * Structured academic collaboration: I don't just sit in study sessions; I build organized outlines, track high-yield concepts, and help break down dense material like genetics or organic chemistry so the group actually retains it.
 * Operational follow-through: When planning events, I manage details like handling scheduling, tracking supplies, and coordinating logistics so things actually run on time instead of falling apart at the last minute.
 * Objective problem-solving: In group settings, I stay level-headed. If there is friction, poor communication, or a project stalling out, I focus on the practical fix rather than getting bogged down in debate.
 * Instructional communication: Having experience teaching and working directly with the public, I know how to explain complex tasks clearly, adapt to different learning styles, and speak effectively when representing the chapter to outside professionals or faculty.
I offer real execution—someone who contributes actionable ideas, keeps commitments organized, and handles the operational side of the fraternity efficiently.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text:
My experiences across hands-on work, instruction, and community service have shaped the practical mindset I will carry into medicine.
At Olympic Barber Shop, assisting in a family business taught me the fundamentals of operational discipline and hygiene protocols. Managing licensing and sanitation showed me that patient safety begins long before a procedure starts—it is built on sterile conditions, regulatory compliance, and consistency in small details. 
Similarly, working in high-volume food service at Mamma Lucia tested my composure under sustained pressure. Coordinating kitchen efficiency and customer orders during peak rushes required quick prioritization, clear communication, and emotional control, all of which are essential in fast-paced clinical settings.  
Teaching Tae Kwon Do at US White Tiger Martial Arts translated those habits into direct leadership and accountability. Instructing groups of over twenty students required diagnosing technical errors in real time, adapting explanations to individual learning curves, and establishing mutual trust. In healthcare, treatment compliance relies heavily on patient education; teaching martial arts taught me how to break down complex physical movements with patience and clarity.  
My humanitarian work with the Appalachia Service Project grounded these skills in the broader realities of community care. Performing critical structural home repairs for underserved families exposed me to the environmental factors that directly influence family well-being. It was demanding physical labor under strict timelines, reinforcing that genuine service requires rolling up your sleeves and meeting people’s fundamental needs directly.  
Together, these roles have taught me how to operate under stress, maintain rigorous standards of hygiene, communicate across diverse backgrounds, and treat service as a responsibility rather than a title. They have provided the discipline, work ethic, and humility necessary to take on the demands of patient care.

notes.brother: From their application: Why this major / passion for healthcare
notes.text:
I chose to major in Biology on the pre-dental track because I've always been drawn to the combination of science, hands-on work, and meaningful relationships that dentistry offers. While exploring various healthcare careers in high school, I realized dentistry was the field where my interests aligned most naturally. I love science, problem-solving, and artistry, and I hope to apply those skills to improve a patient’s health, confidence, and quality of life.

My passion for healthcare is also rooted in my personal background. Growing up, I saw how members of my family struggle with their oral health and witnessed how the effects of poor oral health can affect someone’s confidence and overall well-being. My passion grew further by serving my community in Tampa: through volunteering at food pantries, mobile health clinics, and healthcare organizations, I have seen how closely healthcare is connected to a person’s circumstances and access to resources. These experiences have shown me that being a healthcare professional is not simply about treating a condition, but about listening to patients, understanding their circumstances, and recognizing that everyone’s needs differ based on their background.

As I continue my education, I want to become a dentist who combines strong clinical knowledge with compassion and genuine patient care. Pursuing biology on the pre-dental track gives me the foundation to reach that goal while allowing me to explore the broader healthcare field, learn from those around me, and discover the many opportunities and specialties dentistry offers.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED
notes.text:
I hope to gain a stronger understanding of different healthcare careers while joining a community of students who are equally passionate about pursuing healthcare. As a pre-dental student, I want to use MED to learn from students pursuing different professions and gain perspectives beyond my own path. I am especially excited about the plethora of resources MED provides, whether that's research, healthcare professionals, professional development opportunities, and, most importantly, a sense of community.

I would also love to learn from upperclassmen who have already navigated the challenges of being a prehealth student. They have experienced the academics, applications, shadowing, research, and other opportunities that come with pursuing any healthcare career. I plan to build meaningful connections with members who can challenge me to grow personally and professionally while allowing me to share what I've learned from my own experiences.

Finally, I would love the opportunity to contribute to MED as much as I hope to benefit from it. Service and community are extremely important to me, which has led me to volunteer at mobile health clinics, food pantries, and various community organizations. Knowing that service is such an important part of MED’s brotherhood, I would love to participate in outreach opportunities and share the ones I know are available to make a tangible difference not only in the Tampa Bay community but also in MED. Overall, I would love to leave MED with stronger professional skills, meaningful friendships, new perspectives, and a community that continues to support me throughout my healthcare journey.

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring
notes.text:
I would contribute enthusiasm, strong communication skills, reliability, a genuine commitment to service, and a willingness to learn. Through my volunteer experiences and campus involvement, I have learned how important it is to be someone others can depend on, especially when working with other brothers. One of my strongest qualities is my ability to connect with people. I am naturally bubbly and outgoing, and I love talking with others! This has helped me meet people from different backgrounds and learn to communicate with individuals from all walks of life. These experiences have taught me to be patient, welcoming, and attentive to others' needs. I also bring positive energy to group environments, which would support MED’s professional and social aspects of brotherhood.

Additionally, I bring leadership and organizational experience. Through my involvement in various UTampa student organizations and executive boards, I’ve developed skills in planning, collaboration, communication, outreach, and creating engaging events and content. As co-president of the African Student Association, I've put these skills into practice while navigating the challenges of leading an organization, and I'd love to bring that experience to MED to support outreach, events, and community-building efforts as needed.

Lastly, I am curious and always willing to learn. I don't expect to know everything as I enter MED, but I am excited to learn from my brothers, share my experiences, and support others as we work toward our long- and short-term career goals.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text:
My experiences in community service, employment, and campus involvement have helped me develop the skills required for a healthcare career and made me a better, well-rounded individual.

Through my long-term involvement with ICNA Relief’s Tampa food pantry, I have volunteered for nearly five years and accumulated hundreds of service hours. I have learned the importance of patience, communication, and treating everyone with dignity. Working with the Greater Tampa Bay community has shown me that people seeking assistance may come from very different circumstances, and regardless, empathy and respect should be present in every interaction. Similarly, volunteering with ICNA Relief's mobile health clinics and the Red Crescent clinic has given me exposure to serving patients in community healthcare settings. These experiences have taught me the importance of organization, teamwork, and attention to detail, while strengthening my interest in patient care and showing me the responsibility that comes with working with people who trust you with their care.

As a receptionist, I strengthened my skills by remaining professional and composed when interacting with a wide range of people, addressing concerns, communicating effectively, adapting to unexpected situations, and solving problems in real time. These skills are essential when interacting with patients, families, and healthcare teams.

However, the most impactful and relevant experience was my dental outreach internship with VAW Global Health Alliance in Cusco, Peru, with Hillsborough Community College and UTampa students. I gained hands-on experience assisting dentists, preparing and sterilizing instruments, taking vitals, supporting patient check-in, and organizing supplies. Working directly with patients in a clinical setting, including suctioning and infection control, gave me a realistic understanding of how hands-on and personal dentistry can and will be. Serving underserved communities abroad also showed me how access to healthcare can vary greatly depending on a person's circumstances; this experience strengthened my desire to become a dentist and reminded me of healthcare professionals' responsibility to serve patients with compassion.

Lastly, my involvement in student organizations has developed my leadership, collaboration, and organizational skills. As co-president of ASA, I have learned firsthand how challenging it can be to balance an executive board, plan events, communicate effectively, and manage the organization's responsibilities. Balancing academics, employment, volunteering, and extracurriculars has taught me time management and commitment, showing me that healthcare requires not only knowledge but also qualities you can't learn from a book.

facts: Currently involved in: I am in the Pre-PA club, I intend on volunteering through Spartans Against Homelessness, and I am shadowing a PA at Moffitt Cancer Center in a few weeks.

notes.brother: From their application: Why this major / passion for healthcare
notes.text: There are many reasons why I decided to follow a career in healthcare. Aside from being able to develop meaningful connections with patients and continue to learn and grow throughout my career, I want to help people. There was no switch that went off in my head that led me to the health field, instead, I have encountered various experiences with healthcare workers that have each reinforced my passion. I've met amazing healthcare workers in my life, people with families, people who put the wellbeing of strangers over others. It is inspiring to see people who are truly passionate about their careers, especially when their career is as vital as a healthcare worker. With the growth of AI, many jobs will undoubtably be replaced, yet healthcare- even if robots end up performing surgeries or administering vaccines- contains an extremely important aspect in patient recovery: human connection. Those who work in medicine are not just utilizing medicine and advancements to help improve the quality of life for patients, they are providing each patient with a sense of hope- a sense of belonging. I want to ensure people who are struggling with their health are not only taken care of physically but also taken care of emotionally and mentally.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED
notes.text: I am hoping to gain meaningful connections with brothers and other people in similar positions as me. I think that a huge part of college is finding a community. I believe that MED would serve as an opportunity for me to connect with others, as well as feel more of a sense of belonging within the school. Being that I am pursuing a career in health, it is essential that I find other like-minded students who are driven to be successful, like myself. Aside from developing meaningful connections that will help guide me through my pre-health track, MED provides extensive opportunities to get involved with the community as well as in the health care field. Through their frequent volunteering sessions, I would gain knowledge of the world and grow as a person, learning how I can leave an impact on our community in many ways. I would also have the opportunity to meet people who I would not meet otherwise, learning their stories and pushing me to become the best version of myself possible. The health care opportunities through MED will help with my applications to PA-school, but more importantly, they will teach me about the field I am going to enter. There are many things that I hope to gain from MED, each aspect shaping me as a person and molding me into my best self.

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring
notes.text: My most valuable skill is my ability to empathize with others. This will help me in events through MED, but it will also help me connect with my brothers and become a more well-rounded person. I am also an extremely patient person, especially after years working with children and the elderly. I truly believe patience to be a virtue and that everyone deserves a chance to be heard and appreciated. I think that patience is more than being able to "wait", I think it is a true expression of kindness and an individual's ability to empathize and sympathize with others. I also am a very open-minded person and take critique well and value critique immensely. On top of that, I am very comfortable being in a position of leadership. Lastly, I am social and able to communicate well with others. I have grown drastically as a person since coming to college. I used to be extremely socially anxious and shy, and I believe that makes me even better at communicating. I have learned how to deal with my anxieties and be confident. I can also communicate effectively with people who may have a harder time speaking up, being that I was in their shoes. On the other hand, I can communicate well with outspoken people because I strive to be like them and admire their confidence.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text: I have worked in a retirement home for over three years as a waitress. My job has gifted me valuable lessons and perspectives on life I would have not otherwise gained. When working in a retirement home, it is imperative that you connect with the residents and make them feel as comfortable as possible. Many of the residents have gone through traumatic events, fought in wars, traveled the world, lost their spouses, or even lost their whole families. Even though I waitress at the retirement home, I still have become close to the residents, them claiming me and my coworkers to be their "grandchildren". Seeing so many residents come through the restaurant and building connections with them has showed me that everyone has a story. Being able to sympathize with others is a crucial part of a career in health care. Being that I work with the elderly, many of the residents have passed away, some of which leaving their friends and spouses to grieve. It is heartbreaking to see an elderly woman come into the restaurant alone and have her cry to about how she can't live without her husband. Though death is a part of life, there are many people whose lives are taken too fast. Everyone deserves to life a healthy, long, prosperous life, and I want to do everything in my power to make this possible. As well as working in a retirement home, this summer I volunteered in a hospital, helping patients to move around and socialize. This opportunity has enhanced my communication skills with patients as well as healthcare workers. I've learned vital techniques such as putting on PPE and how to safely aid a patient during movement. Volunteering at a hospital has showed me that everyone is human, no matter their race, sex, religion, etc. When people come to a hospital, they are seeking help, and everyone deserves to have that granted. This hospital volunteer program has helped me grow as a person and taught me more about healthcare.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text: Over the past summer, I was working as a nanny for multiple different families. This job was so rewarding and fulfilling in so many different ways, but I feel that it greatly helped me for my future career goals. I am currently very interested in becoming a pediatric dentist and working primarily with children. Nannying gave me the opportunity to better understand how children with many different personalities think and how they handle their emotions at young ages. This gave me lots of insight into how I might handle a situation in which a child is nervous or upset about going to the dentist because I spent lots of time learning how to calm a meltdown in many different ways. I worked with some kids who were very calm and very rarely experienced big emotions, but I also worked with some kids who tended to have meltdowns over small things quite often. I had to work to adapt and pivot situations in order to distract from the problem. I have spent around 50 hours so far shadowing in a dentist office. This shadowing experience has been extremely valuable in so many different ways. I have had the ability to talk one on one with many different dentists, who have all had different experiences within the field. This has given me more knowledge on what I can expect when I move forward on the dentistry track. While shadowing I had the opportunity to watch routine procedures, such as cavity fillings, routine cleanings, and denture fittings. This was all incredibly valuable for my future career, as I now understand how the common everyday tasks are performed within a dentist office. I also had the opportunity to observe less common procedures such as crown placings and root canals. Crowns fascinated me the most because it is an art to form the tooth. This opened a new potential career path in cosmetic dentistry, because I think that I would love the artistic portions of the work required. Shadowing has been extremely valuable for my future in dentistry as I have learned lots from the personal experiences of the dentists I have shadowed as well as what I have observed of patients and the procedures I have seen.

notes.brother: From their application: Why this major / passion for healthcare
notes.text:
I chose to major in Allied Health - Medical Sciences because I have always been drawn to healthcare, but my passion for optometry is deeply personal. My mother is an optometrist, so I grew up around the field, but one experience in particular shaped the way I see it.
When I was in third grade, I developed a persistent eye tic where I could not stop rolling my eyes. My mom took me to multiple eye doctors and even neurosurgeons, trying to understand what was happening. Eventually after asking the right questions, like "is there anyone you do not want to sit next to in class" she realized that I was being bullied by a girl in my class and that the stress I was experiencing was affecting me physically. That experience has stayed with me and is a big reason why I want to work with children and support both them and their parents. I really appreciate the healthcare world that tries extremely hard to find a solution and treat the root cause of the problem through natural options- before medications, and I hope to continue that holistic practice as a doctor. 
Through shadowing numerous optometrists, I not only solidified my career path, but I have also learned that there is so much more to the eyes than what we see on the surface. Every patient brings something new, and I love that optometry combines science, hands-on care, problem-solving, and meaningful patient relationships.
One doctor once explained that she became an Optometrist because she wanted to protect the sense people fear losing most. That idea has stuck with me, and will for a very long time. I want to become the kind of doctor who not only cares for a patient's vision, but also listens, builds trust, and helps families understand what their child may be experiencing. That is what makes me passionate about healthcare and certain that optometry is the path I want to pursue.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED
notes.text:
What I hope to gain from Mu Epsilon Delta is a community of people who are just as passionate about healthcare, academics, and making a difference as I am. I don’t have many friends who are pursuing healthcare or who are as academically driven, so I want to change that and surround myself with people who motivate me to become better both personally and professionally.

I want MED to be a place where I can find people to study with, struggle and learn alongside, and grow through both our failures and successes. I want to experience the difficult classes, stressful exams, bad grades, and proud moments with people who understand what it is like to work toward a career in healthcare. Having people around me who understand those challenges would make the difficult moments feel a little less overwhelming and the accomplishments even more rewarding.

I also really value MED’s commitment to service, as I want more opportunities to volunteer and give back to my community as an aspiring healthcare professional. I am excited about service experiences where I can meet and help different people, learn about their experiences and needs, and continue to develop the type of healthcare professional I want to be.

Most importantly, I hope to build genuine relationships that last beyond college. I want to meet people who become my friends, mentors, study partners, and eventually colleagues. I hope to contribute to the MED brotherhood just as much as I grow from it, and to leave college with not only meaningful professional connections, but friendships and memories that last a lifetime.

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring
notes.text:
One of the biggest things I would contribute to MED is my ability to connect with people. I genuinely enjoy meeting new people and finding ways to make others feel comfortable and included. I have always been someone who tries to lift the mood when someone’s down, whether that means making someone laugh, starting a conversation with someone who seems shy, or simply making sure no one feels left out. I find it genuinely rewarding when I can bring people together and create an environment where everyone feels welcome.

I also consider myself a very driven and dependable person. I put a lot of effort into anything I care a lot about it and hold myself to a high standard, thus my career and the people I surround myself with is at the top of my list. Pursuing a career in healthcare has taught me that being successful is not just about doing well individually, but also about being willing to learn from others and support the people around you.

I think these qualities would allow me to contribute to the brotherhood in a meaningful way. I would bring positive energy to events and really make an effort to get to know people beyond the surface level and be someone my brothers can rely on. Whether it is studying together, volunteering, planning an event, or simply checking in on someone having a difficult week, I want to be the kind of person who makes the people around me feel supported. I hope to bring both ambition and a genuine sense of community to MED while encouraging the people around me to grow alongside me.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text:
The experiences I have had so far have taught me that working in healthcare requires much more than knowing just chemistry and math and biology… it requires patience, communication, adaptability, attention to detail, and the ability to make patients feel comfortable.
Working as a Clinical Optometric Assistant for over a year gave me my first real experience working directly with patients. I assisted with pre-testing for 15–20 patients a day, operated diagnostic equipment, documented patient information, and learned how important accuracy is when working with someone’s health. Working with young children who may not want to listen, adults who can be more difficult to communicate with, and elderly patients who might have trouble hearing has taught me that every patient communicates and responds differently, and that I need to adjust my approach accordingly.
As a Discover UTampa mentor, I developed this skill even further. I mentored incoming freshmen this year and helped them recognize their own leadership abilities. I learned how to handle different personalities and situations, including students who were disengaged or did not initially want to participate. Instead of expecting everyone to respond to the same approach, I learned to change how I communicated and find different ways to connect with them.
I know this will be extremely important in healthcare since every patient, especially every child, will understand information and respond to treatment differently. As a future optometrist, I will need to recognize those differences and adapt how I explain diagnoses and treatment plans so that patients and their families feel informed and comfortable.
Shadowing different optometrists has also shown me the many responsibilities that comes with being a healthcare provider. These experiences have prepared me to be knowledgeable and dependable, but also compassionate, adaptable, and willing to meet every patient where they are.

notes.brother: From their application: Why this major / passion for healthcare
notes.text: My interest in healthcare came about before I really understood what healthcare even was. Even as a child, I wanted to help others and loved to play “surgery” with my family. When I was eleven, I was hospitalized with appendicitis. The surgeons who treated me were distant, and even sent me home; they thought I was a dramatic young girl and even asked me if my pain was just period cramps. The second time I was admitted to the hospital, I was wary of the doctors and scared I was going to be sent home again. Contrary to my fears, the nurses took the time to explain what was happening to me in words I could understand, checked in consistently, and helped me feel secure. At the time, I didn’t understand the difference, but it left a lasting impression: nurses are the people who are really there for patients. Despite this experience, I still thought I wanted to be a doctor, thinking that becoming a physician was the most direct way to help people in my community. My perspective solidified last year, when my grandfather spent time in a rehabilitation facility after having knee surgery. Through visits with him and reports from my Nana, I was able to see that it was the nurses who cared for him. They assisted him while he regained his ability to walk and helped him manage his pain, caring for him with respect and protecting his dignity.That experience helped me see that nurses provided the direct patient care that I was drawn to. They were present not just for moments after surgery or diagnosis, but as a friendly face throughout treatment. This was the dream I had as a kid; providing care that is consistent, competent, and genuine.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED
notes.text: To me, MED is a symbol of success. It represents the kind of community and commitment I want to center my academic career around. While some of my peers, family, and friends may associate the University of Tampa with its reputation for partying or tanning culture, I want my involvement in MED to demonstrate, both to them and to myself, that I am committed to academic success. I hope to find a group of like-minded individuals I can rely on, when my roommates are going out over the weekend or I need guidance navigating coursework like Chemistry and A&P II. I want to surround myself with people who are driven and dedicated, individuals who can serve as role models throughout my academic journey. Additionally, I hope to find mentors within MED who can guide me through steps like applying for internships and securing faculty mentorship, ultimately modeling to me what it means to be a strong, well-rounded healthcare professional.

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring
notes.text: I believe I can contribute to MED because I am genuinely organized and good at managing my time. I built these skills throughout high school, juggling AP classes and honors classes with sports and extracurriculars. Balancing practices, meets, homework, and club duties helped me learn how to plan ahead instead of just scrambling before deadlines. That habit stuck with me, and I still approach my schedule the same way now. I am also a sociable person who can work well with others. As captain of my high school’s cross country team, I could never only focus on my own performance, I had to keep my teammates motivated and encourage them, which taught me a lot about clear communication and leading by example. Being part of German Club let me connect with people who cared about the same niche as I did, which reminded me how much stronger a community is when it's built around something shared. I was also a student government officer, where I got more practice representing other people, working with different types of groups, and actually following through on projects instead of just talking about them. All of that has made me someone who can handle their own responsibilities while still showing up for a team. I think that a combination of organized, and driven, but also social and collaborative, is what I would bring to MED.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text:
Working at a doctor’s office, I mostly filed papers and sorted through documents. While this taught me a lot about being organized and detail oriented, I also learned that I absolutely did not want a desk job. I consistently felt like I wanted to do more and to have more hands-on experience instead of being confined to a cubicle. I am grateful for the skills that my job gave me, like time management and prioritization, but the feeling of being stuck ultimately pushed me to seek out other opportunities. 
A much more engaging opportunity came to me in an internship. I was a scholarship recipient of Congress Bundestag Youth Exchange’s (CBYX) Vocational program last year. Part of the program was applying for and working at an internship. Through my host dad, who was an oncologist, I was able to be placed in a local hospital on a palliative care ward. There I was able to see the actual rhythm of a hospital shift and was able to experience first hand what it is like to care for and grieve a patient. Even from observing nurses administer medications and perform bedside procedures, I got such an amazing taste of what nursing was really like. Both of these experiences were crucial to my decision of wanting to work in healthcare. It took figuring out what I didn't want to show me what I did; a job where I can make a change in people’s lives and have new experiences every day.

notes.brother: From their application: Why this major / passion for healthcare
notes.text:
I have always had an interest in what is happening beneath the surface of the human body. To me, it is fascinating how complex our bodies are and how so many different systems work together to allow us to live, move, think, and function. Even something as small as a change in the body can have a huge effect on someone’s life. I have always found that interesting and wanted to learn more, which is why I chose to major in Biology and go into medicine.

As I learn more about the human body, I want to use that knowledge to help people. I want to become a doctor who sees each patient as a whole person, not just a diagnosis. Everyone comes from a different background and has different experiences with healthcare, and I want to understand how those experiences can shape the care they need. I want to take the time to get to know my patients and build relationships with them so they feel comfortable talking about what they are going through. I also want to communicate what I know in a way that my patients can understand, especially when they are scared or unsure about what is happening. I want my patients to feel comfortable being honest about what they are experiencing and know that they can have an open conversation with me.

Being a doctor also means being part of a team. Doctors do not work alone they work with nurses and many other healthcare professionals, and everyone brings their own knowledge and experience. I like the idea of being part of a team where everyone works together to give each patient the care and support they need. As I get more experience in healthcare, I am also learning more about the different areas of medicine. I am not set on one specialty yet, and I like that medicine offers so many different possibilities. I want to explore different areas, see what I enjoy, and find where my interests take me.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED
notes.text:
What I’m hoping to gain from MED is a community where I can learn from people who are going through the pre-health process with me. Since MED has students interested in different areas of healthcare, I want to hear about their interests and experiences and learn more about healthcare outside of just the pre-med path. I want to understand what different healthcare professions bring to patient care and why they need to work together.

I also want to learn from upperclassmen who have already been through parts of this process. They have already had to find shadowing, research, and clinical experiences, and I would really value hearing their advice and tips on how they found these opportunities. I also want to hear from people who are getting closer to applying to medical school and learn from what they have experienced so far. From my own experience, finding opportunities can sometimes make me wonder if I’m doing enough or if I’m focusing on the right things. Having people I can ask questions, learn from, and be honest with would mean a lot to me.

I also hope to find a group of people who understand what it is like to be a pre-health student. A lot of my time outside of class goes toward studying, volunteering, and finding ways to prepare for my future career. Sometimes it feels like there is always something else I should be doing, and it can be hard to know if I’m on the right track. I think having people who are going through some of the same things would make the process feel less lonely. I want people I can learn from, support, study with, and also make memories with outside of school.

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring
notes.text:
One thing I would bring to MED is that I am a very organized person. My parents, friends, and especially my roommate always point out how organized and clean I am. Even the professor I mentored noticed this because I would always make sure the lab stayed organized. I like having things in order, and I usually notice when something is messy, unorganized, or could be done better. I think this is something I would naturally bring into MED, especially when planning events, keeping track of things, or helping the group stay organized.

I am also someone who is very determined when I want to figure something out. If my roommate has a problem and asks me for help, I will keep trying to solve it even if I cannot figure it out right away. I’ll keep looking for a way to solve it, even if the first thing I try doesn’t work. Sometimes she even tells me to stop trying to figure it out, but I have a hard time letting a problem go when I know there is probably a solution. I think this is something I could bring to MED when the group is trying to work through a problem or come up with an idea.

I would also bring my experiences as a pre-health student. I have already been involved in volunteering and have been looking for clinical, shadowing, and research opportunities. I would be able to share things I have learned, opportunities I find, and ideas I have with other members. I also genuinely enjoy being around people, so I would want to be involved, get to know the other members, and contribute to the community.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text:
One of the experiences that prepared me the most was volunteering with RAM Clinic. I helped with vision screenings and guided patients through the process. Some patients were nervous or confused, so I learned to introduce myself, explain what I was doing, and ask questions about their vision, such as if they wore glasses or contacts. Many patients were very grateful to have access to the clinic and would thank us for being there. Even though we had to wake up at 3 a.m., I never dreaded going. I enjoyed talking to patients, staying busy, and knowing I was helping people. This experience made me realize how much I enjoy working directly with others.

Being a Chemistry Lab Mentor taught me this in a different way. I learned to notice when students looked confused, even if they did not ask for help. From my own experience, I know that asking a question can sometimes feel intimidating, so I would approach students first and ask if they needed help. I also learned that something that seems simple to me may not be simple to someone else. My professor also noticed how organized I was because I always made sure the lab stayed organized.

Working at Real Hot Yoga taught me how much I enjoy building relationships with people. I got to know regular clients, remembered their names, and enjoyed talking to them when they came in. These experiences have shown me that small things, like introducing yourself, noticing when someone needs help, or remembering someone's name, can make people feel more comfortable. I hope to bring that same mindset into healthcare.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare

I have learned to be patient, dependable, and can think quickly when things don’t go as planned which are very important skills to have in a career in healthcare. Also, I volunteered at a local hospital on a patient floor with nurses for a year and through this experience I gained a better understanding of what it truly means to care for others. First, I learned my way around the hospital and got to explore all the different wings which each had their own unique focus and this made me more interested in pursuing the medical field. I also interacted with many patients and realized healthcare is about a lot more than just medicine. I quickly noticed that many patients were lonely or sad, and that sitting down and talking with them could immediately lift their spirits. This showed me medicine helps a person physically but a friendly face also has a meaningful impact. Finally, during high school I was a member of Thirst project and during my senior year became a co-president. This was a life-changing experience that taught me the valuable lesson to never take what you have for granted because I saw the struggles of not having access to such a simple resource like clean water. Together, these experiences have given me many valuable traits and showed me why I want a career where I can make a difference in people’s lives.

notes.text: My passion for healthcare started as a kid, for a silly reason I'd say. When I was young, I was fascinated by people who got to introduce themselves as "Doctor ***." I was fortunate enough that despite doing contact sports, running around, climbing, lifting, I never sustained a serious injury all the way through my life up to now. Despite my fortune, I have seen others around me, people I care for, get hurt in awful ways. I watched my best friend and teammate of 8 years tear his ACL in front of me, or my wrestling buddy, the kid no one could dislike, I had to watch him break 3 bones in his leg, and all I could do was watch. To watch this my whole life, people in front of me getting hurt, people I care about, and to be able to do nothing but watch, just changed something inside of me. I am the first med student in my family in generations; I could've picked an easier path, one with more familial supports, and maybe even a future position lined up, but I feel an obligation to help those around me with my life, regardless of if it's my best friend or whoever is next to walk in the door.

notes.brother: From their application: What they hope to gain from MED

I am hoping with joining MED that I can find a network of supports to help me as I progress from undergraduate to post-grad applications, whether it be study partners, someone to share experiences with, or just anyone who has more knowledge on the process that they'd be willing to share. Likewise, making some new friends, stepping out of my comfort zone, and just making some memories while also getting aid in my professional development all sound like something I could not pass up on.

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring
notes.text: For starters, I have very good problem-solving skills. I have had this in me my whole life, and while I used to be stubborn and self-centered in the matter, I have evolved to be able to solve problems, alone or among peers very well. I also have picked up good skills with technology, overall using various websites or different commands and functions on computers. One final skill I have good aptitude for is just mediation. While this may fall hand in hand with problem solving, mediation is more a social of a social aspect that I am very good at. In a social group such as a fraternity, having a mediator for problems, to help opposing sides of a debate reach an agreement, or to help decisions being made in a fair way, can be helpful.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text: The job I work at home doesn't align particularly well with my future career path, as in what I actually do, but I have learned valuable skills. The food industry can be a particularly hectic business, with guest complaints and constant orders, stress can be flowing at all times. I admit that before this line of work, I hadn't had much experience with having a boss, and a team that relies on my presence, whether directly needing help with my specific job, or supporting others around me who keep the production flowing. Throughout my time with this I have learned how to be a part of team, whether that requires picking up someone else's slack, or depending on others if I can't keep up. Furthermore, I have learned how to push my pride aside, and to simply do what is needed of me. I don't have to agree with it, I can challenge the concept internally, but I just simply have to do what is needed, which is an apparent skill needed in the medical chain of command. Despite that job being a majority of experience I have in actual work terms, I did some work with the Red Cross Blood Drive in my area, in which I have learned firsthand how to organize and properly format appointments, patient needs, and have gained the ability to adapt to blunders that appear.

notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare

notes.brother: From their application: Skills and traits they'd bring
notes.text: I believe my communication skills and easygoing personality would allow me to contribute to MED. This makes it easy for me to work with different personalities and get along with almost anyone. I am also someone who cares deeply about my friends and consistently supports and looks out for them. notes.brother: From their application: Experience preparing them for healthcare
notes.text:
Working in ocean rescue has prepared me for healthcare by teaching me how to stay calm and act when someone's safety depends on me. I have completed more than 250 rescues and responding to near drownings where victims lost consciousness. I have also helped people fainting from heat stress and treated cuts, head injuries, and marine-life stings. As a head guard, I have added responsibility of leading other guards, communicating clearly, and helping keep our response organized during emergencies. These situations have taught me to remain alert, adjust quickly, and make sure my team is working together. I have also learned from my coworkers with military, emergency medical, and firefighting experience. Seeing how they approach difficult situations has helped me become more disciplined and confident during emergencies.

My hurricane relief work in western North Carolina showed me another side of helping people. Along with cleaning damaged areas, we listened to victims, comforted them, and prayed with those who wanted us to. That experience taught me that people going through a crisis may need emotional support just as much as physical help.

Sports have also played a major role in preparing me for healthcare. I have played sports throughout my life, served as a team captain for two years in high school, and played travel lacrosse for 10 years. These experiences have taught me how to communicate, handle pressure, hold myself accountable, and work towards a shared goal. Healthcare requires many of these same qualities because professionals must trust one another and work together for their patients. Together these experiences have prepared me to take responsibility, remain composed, and care for people during difficult moments.

facts: Familiar with a current brother: The only current MED members I am familiar with are Aidan Nolan and Jayden Pedro, as they are both in my Anatomy & Physiology course this semester.
